The Theory-Theory of concepts is a view of how concepts are structured, acquired, and deployed. Concepts, as they will be understood here, are mental representations that are implicated in many of our higher thought processes, including various forms of reasoning and inference, categorization, planning and decision making, and constructing and testing explanations. The view states that concepts are organized within and around theories, that acquiring a concept involves learning such a theory, and that deploying a concept in a cognitive task involves theoretical reasoning, especially of a causal-explanatory sort.

The term “Theory-Theory” derives from Adam Morton (1980), who proposed that our everyday understanding of human psychology constitutes a kind of theory by which we try to predict and explain behaviour in terms of its causation by beliefs, intentions, emotions, traits of character, and so on. The idea that psychological knowledge and understanding might be explained as theory possession also derives from Premack & Woodruff’s famous 1978 article, “Does the Chimpanzee Have a Theory of Mind?” A Theory-Theory in general is thus a proposal to explain a certain psychological capacity in terms of a tacit or explicit internally represented theory of a domain. The Theory-Theory of concepts, however, goes beyond the mere claim that we possess such theories, saying in addition that some or all of our concepts are constituted by their essential connections with these theories.

The origins of the Theory-Theory involve several converging lines of investigation. First, it arose as part of a general critique of the formerly dominant prototype theory of concepts; second, it was an empirically-motivated response to the shortcomings of the developmental theories of Piaget and Vygotsky; and third, it involved applying ideas from Kuhn’s philosophy of science to explain phenomena having to do with the development of cognition in individuals. While the theory has often been vaguely formulated, due in large part to the open-endedness inherent in the central notion of a theory, there are substantial bodies of empirical evidence that underlie the main tenets of the view. In particular, the Theory-Theory has been responsible for largely displacing the notion that cognitive development starts from a simple base of perceptual primitives grouped together by similarity. Rather, it is guided by domain-specific explanatory expectations at many stages, and these expectations can be seen to function in adult reasoning and categorization as well. While strong versions of the Theory-Theory have been subject to numerous objections, these contributions endure and continue to shape what many scholars claim are the best existing models of higher cognition.
passages.V2:
If there is one thing politicians agree on these days, it is that manufacturing jobs are “good” jobs. (...) Some leaders claim that huge subsidies for new factories will transform the outlook for workers. Others propose tariffs on foreign goods to get more wrenches into people’s hands. Politicians across the rich world believe that reversing the decades-long decline in manufacturing employment would leave workers better off. …

The argument that manufacturing jobs are better than other sorts has a long pedigree. Adam Smith deemed manufacturing “productive,” unlike services. The factories of the Industrial Revolution (...) were also awful places to work: both dangerous and mind-numbingly dull. Things did not improve much with the rise of mass production in the early 20th century. Though relatively well paid, workers in car plants complained about monotony. As one put it, “If I keep putting on Nut Number 86 for about 86 more days, I will be Nut Number 86 in the bughouse.” Even during the post-war period, people were hardly thrilled to toil in factories. (...) In 1970 Fortune magazine coined the phrase “blue-collar blues” to describe the alienation many manufacturing workers felt. One pundit noted they would be “easy prey for demagogues.”

Manufacturing enthusiasts counter that jobs in the sector are much better today. Workplace accidents occur far less often. Most factories are air-conditioned. Robots do many of the heaviest, most repetitive tasks. And around a third of those employed in manufacturing perform white-collar roles such as design and engineering. But compare workers of similar education levels and there is little evidence they would gain by moving from services to manufacturing. One paper from America’s Bureau of Labour Statistics found that, across a variety of measures including pay, benefits, job security and safety, “many industries within services equal or exceed manufacturing.” (...) Similar findings have emerged from data in Britain, suggesting that job quality in the manufacturing sector is no better than average. For decades economists observed that manufacturing workers enjoyed a wage premium over comparable workers in other industries. A recent paper published by the Federal Reserve shows that this premium has “disappeared.” Those who point to the insecurity of gig jobs … would do well to remember that manufacturing roles can be more cyclical than those in services. They are also more likely to be automated away. It is not obvious that tending an industrial robot is more satisfying than operating an espresso machine, especially for those who enjoy human interaction.

One prominent politician declared: “A job is about a lot more than a pay cheque. It’s about your dignity. It’s about respect.” Indeed. Yet dignity and respect should be available wherever people are employed. Politicians might do better to ensure that any job—no matter the sector—offers the stability and respect workers crave. If not, they risk spending billions trying to recreate a past that was far less rosy than they imagine. Companies have a role to play, too, and there is ample evidence that employers who treat workers well reap rewards. The notion that manufacturing is always superior to services does not hold up. Workers themselves must face that nostalgia misleads. Work can be a drag, but it is probably the best it has ever been.
passages.V3:
In the late 19th century, whalers, settlers and pirates changed the ecology of the Galápagos Islands by poaching some native species—like Galápagos giant tortoises—and introducing others, like goats and rats. The latter species became pests and severely destabilized the island ecosystems. Goats overgrazed the fruits and plants the tortoises ate, while rats preyed on their eggs. Over time, the tortoise population plummeted. On Española, an island in the southeast of the archipelago, the tortoise count fell from over 10,000 to just 14. Along the way, with goats eating all the plants they could, Española—once akin to a savanna—turned barren. A century later, conservationists set out to restore the Galápagos giant tortoise on Española—and the island ecosystem. They began eradicating the introduced species and capturing Española’s remaining tortoises and breeding them in captivity. With the goats wiped out and the tortoises in cages, the ecosystem transformed once again. This time, the overgrazed terrain became overgrown with densely packed trees and woody bushes. Española’s full recovery to its savanna-like state would have to wait for the tortoises’ return.

From the time those 14 tortoises were taken into captivity between 1963 and 1974 until they were finally released in 2020, conservationists reintroduced nearly 2,000 captive-bred Galápagos giant tortoises to Española. Since then, the tortoises have continued to breed in the wild, causing the population to blossom to an estimated 3,000. They’ve also seen the ecology of Española transform once more as the tortoises are reducing the extent of woody plants, expanding the grasslands and spreading the seeds of a key species. The tortoises’ return has also helped the critically endangered waved albatross—a species that breeds exclusively on Española. During the island’s woody era, people had to repeatedly clear the areas the seabirds use as runways to take off and land. Now, if the landing strips are getting overgrown, they’ll move tortoises into the area to take care of it for them. The secret to this success is that giant tortoises are ecological architects. As they browse, poop and plod about, they alter the landscape. They trample young trees and bushes before they can grow big enough to block the albatrosses’ way.

To study these impacts up close, researchers fenced off some of the island’s cactuses, which gave them a way to assess how the landscapes evolve when they’re either exposed to or free from the tortoises’ influences. They also studied satellite imagery of the island captured between 2006 and 2020 and found that while parts of the island are still seeing an increase in the density of bushes and trees, places where the tortoises have rebounded are more open and savanna-like. As few as one or two tortoises per hectare, the scientists believe, is enough to trigger a shift in the landscape. While the findings line up with what conservationists expected, it was nice to have their suspicions confirmed. The results bode well for other rewilding projects that include giant tortoise restoration as a keystone of their efforts, such as those underway on other islands in the Galápagos archipelago and on the Mascarene Islands in the Indian Ocean.
passages.V4:
Sixty years after her death, Édith Piaf’s voice will be re-created using AI to narrate her biopic. Warner Music Group has partnered with the Piaf estate to produce the feature-length film Edith. AI has been trained to replicate Piaf’s voice by feeding it hundreds of voice clips, with the re-creation promising to “enhance the authenticity and emotional impact of her story.” Animation will provide “a modern take” on the La Vie en Rose singer’s life, (...) The film is at a proof-of-concept stage and will include archival footage, personal moments and interviews. Piaf’s original performances will also be featured, with no announcement that the AI tech will develop new music. Julie Veille, who directed documentaries on Diana Ross and Stevie Wonder, conceived the project. ‘If Édith were still with us, what messages would she want to convey?’” she said. “Her story is one of incredible resilience, of overcoming struggles and defying social norms to achieve greatness - and is as relevant now as it was then. (...) Our goal is to utilise the latest advancements in technology to bring the timeless story to audiences. “

The executors of Piaf’s estate said: “It’s been a special and touching experience to be able to hear Édith’s voice once again - the technology has made it feel like we were back in the room with her. (...) Through this film we’ll be able to show the real side of Édith - her joyful personality, her humour and her unwavering spirit.” It’s not the first time a dead artist has returned as a narrator: Andy Warhol’s voice was recreated via AI for The Andy Warhol Diaries, with an actor’s reading morphed into Warhol’s voice to produce a 21st-century imagining of the robot version of himself. Actor Edward Herrmann was also brought back to narrate newly published audiobooks. The practice proved controversial when used in a documentary about Anthony Bourdain, where software trained on Bourdain’s voice recreated an email he had sent to a friend. An ersatz Bourdain reflected: “My life is sort of shit now. You are successful, and I am successful, and I’m wondering: Are you happy?” Morgan Neville, the director, said viewers might not realise the sleight of hand. Critics included Bourdain’s ex-wife, who wrote: “I certainly was NOT the one who said Tony would have been cool with that.”

In music, John Lennon’s voice was recently isolated via AI software to help the surviving Beatles record Now and Then, described as their final song together. Paul McCartney stressed the software wasn’t used to create a new Lennon performance: “Nothing has been artificially or synthetically created,” he said. “It’s all real, and we all play on it. We cleaned up some existing recordings.” But AI is increasingly being used to make entirely original performances by vocalists, whose voices train software that then creates uncanny replicas. In April, Drake said “this is the final straw” after an AI version of him appeared in a fake performance of music by Ice Spice. That same month, a song featuring AI-created vocals of Drake and the Weeknd was pulled from streaming. (...) Critics argue that such creations cross ethical and legal lines, sparking debates about the future of artists’ rights.

When did the ‘modern’ era begin? For the European imagination, the most significant divide was between antiquity and what followed, such that for centuries ‘modern history’ was held to have begun with the fall of Rome. The category of the ‘Middle Ages’ indicated an epoch between the ancient world and the ‘revival’ of learning, with the late 15th century then becoming the first modern era. In both cases, the criteria were intellectual, political and religious. From the late 18th century onwards, the most alert observers sensed there was a new type of society—new not just in Europe, but in human history. Societies based on agriculture, crafts and subsistence were replaced by those based on commerce, industry and abundance.

The concept of the modern era has shifted from a post-Roman intellectual and political framework to recognizing a global transformation in societal structure and economy.
European perceptions of the modern era have evolved from intellectual and political definitions to acknowledging the broader global shift from agrarian to industrial societies.
The modern era was initially defined by the revival of learning after the fall of Rome, but by the 18th century, observers recognized a new societal structure based on industry and commerce.

17.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Laughing and crying are some of the most familiar experiences any of us have, and they stretch back before the most nebulous depths of childhood. But laughing and crying are also highly ambiguous. Consider how other expressions that mobilize the body and the face—rubbing the belly to indicate hunger, shaking a fist to show anger or threat—translate an intention or need into bodily language. But that’s not the case with laughing and crying. They aren’t symbolic, they just are. They are also universal across cultures and essentially human. Stereotyped and genuine, universal and private, physical and mental: laughing and crying are, paradoxically, all of the above. Both possess a quotidian self-evidence; yet when treated as a dilemma, what are laughing and crying? Which branch of knowledge is even responsible for them? Psychology? Anthropology? Aesthetics, neuroscience, physiology, philosophy?
opts: Laughing and crying are paradoxical expressions that are universal but ambiguous, raising questions about their meaning across cultures.
Unlike other bodily expressions that symbolize specific needs, laughing and crying are enigmatic yet universally human experiences studied across multiple fields.
Laughing and crying, though familiar and universal in humans, are without symbolism but deeply ambiguous, posing questions about what they are.
Laughing and crying are common but paradoxical experiences, both universal and ambiguous, leaving us unsure about their place in human understanding.

Instead of being organized around information, the contemporary internet is organized around content: exchangeable packets, unweighted by the truthfulness of their substance. Unlike knowledge, all content is flat. None is more or less justified in ascertaining true belief. None of it, at its core, is information. As a result, our lives are consumed with the consumption of content, but we no longer know the truth when we see it. And when we don’t know how to weigh different truths, or to coordinate among different real-world experiences to look behind the veil, there is either cacophony or a single victor: a loudest voice that wins.

The organisation around content over information on the internet results in the absence of a hierarchy of truth allowing the loudest voice to control perception.
Content on the internet lacks the depth of information and knowledge, leading to societal confusion, competing truths, and the rise of authoritative voices.
